# Full Stop {#sec-full-stop}

| I didn't choose to stop. No choice was made.
| I just didn't open it next evening, or the one after.
| The evenings went to the tool, as for months, and stayed.
| Nobody noticed, me included, thereafter.
| The wall above my desk stayed empty. There
| The pin holes still are, in pairs. And then, from Red,
| The email quoting line six hundred and twelve, where,
| Having read the README twice, he asked, instead,
| "Is there a book in here?" He meant the three
| Years, and the tool, and me. I said I didn't know,
| Then started this one, which is how I'd see.
| The first night, I ran the tool on it. Little to show,
| It found one problem, with its chapter and its line:
| This book said "eleven chapters". This book has nine.

| The tool, which I had built for Full Stop, and had run
| On Full Stop a thousand times, had flagged as wrong
| Full Stop's own number. I looked a while; then, in one
| Line of a note, I told it where that count did belong:
| Another book. That note was the first I fed
| The tool, of Full Stop, that wasn't a gripe. I ran
| It once again: nothing. As the preface said,
| This book was written with the tool. Since it began,
| It read each night each chapter, through and through,
| Against what the book had promised, and would show
| Me when one disagreed. Several times, it's true,
| It told me. I fixed most of them. And so:
| A tool built to avoid a book can still be how a book gets finished.
| It just isn't the book it was built for.

| Full Stop has eleven chapters. It still does.
| Chapter four still credits its shop, and nine
| Still credits the rival, all just as it was;
| The footnotes still point at each other, down the line.
| I've stopped minding. The shoeboxes are in a closet. There,
| In one of them, is the card from behind the radiator, I know;
| I'm still not sure where. Last week, Hedda turned her chair
| Away from her monitor, with four minutes to go,
| And asked how the book was.

| "Which one?"
| I said.

| She wrote that down.
